name: Anani
title: Descendant of David in the post-exilic period
summary: In the Davidic genealogy in 1 Chronicles, Anani is listed as the youngest of Eljoenai's seven sons and the last person named in the royal lineage from David. Through Solomon and Zerubbabel, he belonged to the line that carried forward the covenant promise of an eternal kingdom. The fact that the genealogy ends with his name makes him a key figure for dating the books of Chronicles and for understanding questions about Davidic messianic expectations in the post-exilic Jewish community. The name Anani may mean "the Lord has answered" or be connected to the Aramaic word for "cloud," which has given rise to speculation about links to prophetic descriptions of a coming heavenly figure. The careful preservation of this lineage through generations testifies to a deep conviction that God's promise to David remained valid, even in a time without royal power in Israel.

keyEvents.title: Listed in David's genealogy
keyEvents.description: Anani is mentioned as the last of the seven sons of Eljoenai in the Davidic genealogy. His placement at the very end of the genealogy makes him the last known named individual in David's royal line as presented in the Old Testament.

keyEvents.title: The Davidic lineage from Zerubbabel to Anani
keyEvents.description: Anani belongs to the last known generation of the royal Davidic line continued from Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile. The fact that the author of Chronicles extends this genealogy so far forward in time testifies to a deliberate theological intention to document God's faithfulness to the covenant promise made to David.

versions.summary: Anani was a descendant of King David through the line of Zerubbabel, mentioned in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Eljoenai and represented one of the last known generations in the Davidic royal house after the return from exile in Babylon. Some scholars have speculated whether his name may be linked to messianic expectations following the exile.
versions.title: Descendant of David
versions.reason: [major] Anani is not described as a 'leader' in the Bible. He is mentioned only as a descendant of David in a genealogy. The role 'descendant of David' or 'member of David's lineage' is more accurate. There is no biblical evidence that he held a leadership function.; [minor] The second key event ('David's royal lineage') overlaps significantly with the fourth ('Lineage after Zerubbabel'). Verses 1, 10, 16, 17, and 19 in 1 Chronicles 3 deal with various parts of the genealogy, but Anani himself is not mentioned in these verses. It may be more accurate to combine these or tighten the references.; [minor] According to 1 Chronicles 3:24, Elioenai had seven sons. The six siblings listed (Hodaviah, Eljasib, Pelajah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah) match in number with Anani being the seventh. The names should be carefully verified against the original text but appear largely correct.; [major] Footnotes are missing. The profile should include at least one footnote explaining the linguistic meaning of the name Anani, the possible messianic connection (mentioned in the summary), or the historical context for the Davidic lineage after the exile.; [minor] Four key events for a person mentioned in only one verse is excessive. They overlap significantly. It would have been better to have two clearly distinct events rather than four that largely cover the same information.

versions.title: Descendant of David in the post-exilic period
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 ('Anani was a descendant of King David through the line of Zerubbabel, mentioned in 1 Chronicles. He was...'). Since there is one earlier version, the text should be rephrased more clearly to avoid repetition.; [minor] In the second key event, verses 19, 21, 22, 23, and 24 from 1 Chron 3 are included. Verse 20 also contains relevant names in Zerubbabel's line and should be considered for inclusion for completeness. Alternatively, the reference could be tightened to include only the most relevant verses concerning Anani himself.; [minor] The dating 'c. 500s BC' is possible, but the footnotes themselves note that some textual traditions shift the dating toward the 400s BC. It may be more precise to use a somewhat broader time estimate such as 'c. 500–400s BC' to reflect this uncertainty.; [minor] The role 'descendant of David' is correct, but could be supplemented with, for example, 'part of the royal lineage' to add depth.; [minor] Verse 20 in 1 Chron 3 belongs to Zerubbabel's sons and is part of the same continuous genealogy. Its omission is not an error, but consider including it.

versions.summary: Anani is the last named person in the Davidic genealogy in 1 Chronicles. As the son of Eljoenai and the youngest of his seven sons, he belonged to the royal lineage from David through Solomon and Zerubbabel. His placement in the genealogy makes him one of the last known representatives of David's royal house in the period after the return from Babylon. The name Anani may mean "the Lord has answered" or be linked to the Aramaic word for "cloud," and several scholars have seen a possible connection to messianic expectations that lived on in the Jewish community during this period. That the author of Chronicles carefully traces this lineage all the way to his own time underscores the conviction of God's faithfulness in preserving David's line in accordance with the covenant promise.
versions.title: Descendant of David in the post-exilic period
versions.reason: [minor] In 1 Chr 3:24, the sons of Eljoenai are listed as Hodavja, Eljasib, Pelaja, Akkub, Johanan, Delaja and Anani. The order appears correct, but the name 'Hodavja' should be verified – some textual traditions have 'Hodavjahu'. The most common form in Norwegian Bible tradition is 'Hodavja', so this is acceptable.; [minor] The summary is well phrased, but resembles earlier versions in its opening structure ('Anani is the last named person in the Davidic genealogy in 1 Chronicles'). To distinguish itself more clearly from previous attempts, the introduction should be rephrased somewhat.; [minor] The two key events overlap thematically quite considerably. The second event ('The Davidic lineage after Zerubbabel') covers a broad scope and repeats much of the content from the first. A clearer differentiation would strengthen the profile.

footnotes.text: The name Anani (Hebrew: עֲנָנִי, 'Anani') is likely a short form of Ananiah and means 'The Lord has answered' or 'The Lord's cloud.' Some scholars have connected the name with the Aramaic word for 'cloud' and seen a possible link to Daniel 7:13, where 'one like a son of man' comes with the clouds of heaven. This has led to speculation about messianic expectations associated with this person in the post-exilic period.

In the Davidic genealogy in 1 Chronicles 3, Anani represents one of the very last generations listed. Scholars have used this to date the completion of the books of Chronicles, since the genealogy likely reflects the author's own time. The dating of Anani varies between approximately the 500s and 400s BC, depending on generational calculations from Zerubbabel and which textual tradition is followed.

In some rabbinic sources and in the Septuagint textual tradition, there are variants of the genealogy in 1 Chron. 3:21–24 that may present a somewhat different picture of the generations between Zerubbabel and Anani. Some textual traditions count more generations, which could shift the dating of Anani down toward the 400s BC.

The Elephantine papyri from the fifth century BC mention a Jewish leader named Anani, and although identification with the biblical Anani is uncertain, some scholars have proposed a possible connection. These papyri provide valuable insight into Jewish diaspora life in Egypt during the post-exilic period.

The fact that the author of Chronicles extends David's lineage all the way to his own time underscores the theological conviction that God's covenant promise to David (2 Sam 7:12–16) still stood, even after the monarchy had fallen. The careful preservation of the genealogy points to a living hope for a future restoration of the Davidic line.
